WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Tim Geithner may be the latest political piñata in Washington these days, but -- policy aside -- there may be another reason he is the one fellow everyone is picking on at Treasury: He's there alone. President Obama's ethics code requires that no lobbyist can work for an agency he may have lobbied. Believe it or not, Geithner is the only confirmed official at his department. Some top nominees, even those who have served in government before, have decided to withdraw. Others are still pending as they go through arduous background checks that one pro-Obama Democrat calls "maddening vetting hell." Sure, this is about extensive scrutiny to make sure no one has a tax problem after Geithner's own embarrassing unpaid tax bill. But the staffing problem is not just at Treasury, and it goes way beyond the time-consuming nature of extensive background checks. It's also about overreaching anti-lobbyist rules. Consider Tom Malinowski. He's the advocacy director for Human Rights Watch, an expert on genocide and torture. But when it came time for a top human rights job at the State Department, he was turned away. Why? "Because he lobbied against torture," says one incredulous administration official. "It's crazy." But the rules are the rules: The ethics code requires that no lobbyist can be hired to work for an agency he may have lobbied. So, just to clarify: Someone like Malinowski who lobbied against torture and is a widely acknowledged expert on international human rights law is, er, blackballed. More to the point, he was shown the door precisely because he tried to influence Congress on an issue that both he and the administration agree, and care deeply about. (Malinowski won't comment.) Only in the Alice-in-Wonderland world of Washington would this make any sense. And it still doesn't. It's just a prime instance of the problems that can arise when great-sounding (theoretical) campaign one-liners rub up against the (real) difficulties of trying to staff a government. In other words, the short-term interest in demonizing all lobbyists has led to some very difficult staffing problems. So, if you're an environmental expert and lobbyist, forget about the Environmental Protection Agency. But you might want to think about some work in the health field. That is, unless someone says you're a lucky exception! They're rare, but William Lynn is one. He's a top defense department appointee who once worked as a lobbyist for Raytheon, a military contractor. The White House says that (a) it hasn't had much trouble staffing the government and (b) is willing to make reasonable exceptions. So far we have only seen a handful. The problem has made it difficult to operate at every department. "A lot of good people just can't go into government," says one administration official. "It's a huge departure from the spirit of what they wanted." Indeed, he adds, here's an unintended consequence: "We're setting up a system where the only people who qualify to work in government are the ones who never actually left government." Oh, great. So instead of getting the best and the brightest from finance and elsewhere, we're recycling some folks from Capitol Hill. Not that they're unqualified, but the administration needs input from multiple sources -- outside of Washington. On top of that, the Treasury has another public relations problem: The appointment of anyone with any tie to a bank that has been bailed out or any institution that is tied to the mortgage mess is a non-starter. No wonder it's hard to find the experts. Yet much of this problem is self-inflicted. The no-lobbyist rule could have been "softened" to exclude nonprofit lobbyists. The administration decided against that, one senior official tells me. "We didn't want to label people as 'good lobbyists' or 'bad lobbyists.' " Besides, he adds, "We think we are flexible." That's not the feeling you get speaking with either those jumping hoops to try to get into government and those who have been turned away. As the administration faces its huge economic crisis, it needs all hands on deck. After all, you can't rebuild public confidence in a government if you don't have one.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Tim Geithner may be the latest political piñata in Washington these days, but—policy aside—there may be another reason he has become the target of everyone's frustration at Treasury: he is there alone. President Obama's ethics code prohibits any lobbyist from working for an agency he or she may have lobbied. Remarkably, Geithner remains the only confirmed official at his department. Several top nominees, including some with prior government experience, have chosen to withdraw their names. Others remain in limbo as they undergo exhaustive background checks that one pro-Obama Democrat describes as "maddening vetting hell."

To be fair, this heightened scrutiny is partly designed to ensure no other nominee stumbles into a tax controversy of the sort that embarrassed Geithner himself. But the staffing crisis extends well beyond Treasury, and its roots run deeper than the mere time-consuming nature of background checks. At its core lies an overly broad set of anti-lobbyist restrictions.

Consider the case of Tom Malinowski, advocacy director for Human Rights Watch and a recognized expert on genocide and torture. When a senior human rights position opened at the State Department, he was turned away. Why? "Because he lobbied against torture," one incredulous administration official explains. "It's crazy." Yet the rules are unambiguous: the ethics code bars any lobbyist from being hired by an agency he or she may have lobbied. To clarify the absurdity: a man who campaigned against torture and is widely regarded as an authority on international human rights law finds himself effectively blacklisted. He was shown the door precisely because he sought to influence Congress on an issue that both he and the administration profess to care about deeply. (Malinowski declined to comment.)

Only in the Alice-in-Wonderland logic of Washington could this make sense—and even there, it barely does. It is a striking illustration of what happens when compelling campaign rhetoric collides with the messy realities of actually staffing a government. In short, the short-term political benefit of demonizing all lobbyists has created serious long-term staffing headaches.

So if you're an environmental expert who once lobbied on environmental issues, the Environmental Protection Agency is off-limits—though you might have better luck in the health sector. Unless, of course, you happen to be a "lucky exception." Such exceptions are rare, but William Lynn is one: a senior Defense Department appointee who previously lobbied for Raytheon, a major military contractor.

The White House insists that it has not encountered significant staffing difficulties and remains open to reasonable exceptions. Yet so far, only a handful have been granted. The resulting bottleneck has hampered operations across virtually every department. "A lot of good people just can't go into government," one administration official laments. "It's a huge departure from the spirit of what they wanted." He points to an unintended consequence: "We're setting up a system where the only people who qualify to work in government are the ones who never actually left government."

That is hardly an encouraging outcome. Rather than drawing the best and brightest from finance and other sectors, the administration risks simply recycling personnel from Capitol Hill. Not that such individuals lack qualifications—but effective governance requires perspectives from beyond Washington's own corridors.

Compounding the problem, Treasury faces an additional public relations dilemma: any candidate with ties to a bailed-out bank or an institution linked to the mortgage crisis is essentially disqualified from consideration. Small wonder, then, that finding qualified experts has proven so difficult.

Much of this predicament, however, is self-inflicted. The no-lobbyist rule could have been softened to exempt nonprofit advocates, but the administration chose not to pursue that path. "We didn't want to label people as 'good lobbyists' or 'bad lobbyists,'" one senior official told me. "Besides," he added, "we think we are flexible." That is not, however, the impression one gets from speaking with either those struggling to clear the hurdles to public service or those who have been turned away altogether.

As the administration confronts an economic crisis of historic proportions, it needs all hands on deck. After all, you cannot rebuild public confidence in government if you don't first have one in place.

# The Perils of Idealism: How Ethics Rules Have Stalled the Obama Administration's Staffing Efforts

Nearly three months into his presidency, Barack Obama faces an unexpected bureaucratic crisis: he cannot adequately staff his own administration. The situation at the Treasury Department has become emblematic of this broader problem. Tim Geithner remains, remarkably, the sole confirmed official at an agency tasked with managing the worst financial crisis in generations. This isn't due to a lack of qualified candidates, but rather a direct consequence of Obama's own ethics code, which broadly bars lobbyists from working for agencies they may have previously lobbied. The very rules designed to promote transparency and prevent conflicts of interest have created a paradox: they are keeping experienced, qualified professionals out of the agencies where their expertise is most needed.

The problem has been compounded by heightened scrutiny following Geithner's own tax controversy during his confirmation process. In the aftermath of that embarrassing episode, background checks for nominees have become exhaustive to the point of dysfunction. One frustrated Democrat has described the process as a "maddening vetting hell," a phrase that captures the sense of bureaucratic paralysis now gripping the administration. Nominees who might otherwise be confirmed within weeks find themselves mired in seemingly endless investigations, financial disclosures, and reviews, leading many qualified candidates to simply withdraw their names from consideration rather than endure the process.

Yet the issue extends far beyond the sluggishness of vetting procedures. At its core, the staffing crisis stems from anti-lobbyist rules that are simply too broad in their application. Rather than targeting genuine conflicts of interest, the rules have created blanket prohibitions that disqualify individuals based on the subject matter of their advocacy, regardless of the nature or intent of that advocacy.

Perhaps no case better illustrates this absurdity than that of Tom Malinowski. As a respected human rights expert, Malinowski had spent years lobbying Congress against the use of torture, advocating for policies that align precisely with the values the Obama administration claims to champion. Yet when he was considered for a human rights position at the State Department, his very qualification became his disqualification. The fact that he had lobbied on human rights and torture, issues at the heart of the job he sought, was enough to bar him from consideration under the administration's own ethics rules. In a cruel irony, expertise gained through advocacy became a liability rather than an asset.

This case exposes a broader tension between campaign idealism and governing pragmatism. Obama's ethics rules were crafted with genuine good intentions, an effort to distance his administration from the perception of undue influence and revolving-door politics that has long plagued Washington. But in practice, these rules have produced consequences that seem to contradict common sense. The most qualified candidates, individuals whose careers have been spent advocating for the very causes the administration wishes to advance, are being systematically excluded simply because their expertise was developed through lobbying.

The result is a government administration struggling to fill critical positions, not because of a shortage of talent, but because its own ethical framework has proven too rigid to accommodate the practical realities of governance. As the Malinowski case demonstrates, when idealistic principles are applied without sufficient nuance, they can produce outcomes that undermine the very goals they were meant to serve.

# Obama's Ethics Rules Leave Treasury Department Understaffed as Vetting Process Stalls

More than seven weeks into his presidency, Barack Obama's administration finds itself in an unusual predicament: the Treasury Department, one of the most critical agencies for navigating the ongoing financial crisis, remains staffed by a skeleton crew. Timothy Geithner stands as the only Senate-confirmed official at Treasury, forced to manage an unprecedented economic emergency largely on his own while dozens of key deputy and undersecretary positions sit vacant.

The reason for this staffing vacuum can be traced directly back to one of Obama's signature campaign promises: a strict ethics code designed to curb the influence of lobbyists in government. Under the rules, individuals who have lobbied a particular agency within the past two years are barred from taking a job at that same agency. The policy was crafted as a direct response to public frustration with the revolving door between K Street and federal agencies, and it was meant to signal a clean break from the perceived corruption of the previous administration.

In principle, the rule sounds like sound governance—a way to ensure that officials aren't beholden to the very industries they are meant to regulate. In practice, however, it has created a bureaucratic nightmare. The pool of qualified candidates with relevant financial and economic expertise is inherently limited, and many of the most experienced professionals in banking, finance, and economic policy have, at some point, lobbied on issues related to the very agencies now trying to recruit them. This has left the vetting process bogged down, as nominees are forced to navigate a labyrinth of waivers, disclosures, and legal reviews just to determine whether they qualify under the new restrictions.

The unintended consequences of this policy became glaringly apparent in the case of Tom Malinowski, a respected human rights advocate who was under consideration for a position at the State Department. Malinowski, who had spent years lobbying against the use of torture and advocating for human rights protections, found himself disqualified from serving in the very government he sought to help reform—not because of any conflict of interest in the traditional sense, but simply because his past advocacy work technically classified him as a "lobbyist" under the new rules. The absurdity of barring a human rights champion from public service because he had lobbied against torture underscored just how broadly and inflexibly the ethics code was being applied.

Critics of the policy argue that such cases reveal a fundamental flaw in translating idealistic campaign rhetoric into workable governance. What sounded like a straightforward anti-corruption measure on the campaign trail has, in execution, become a rigid and sometimes nonsensical barrier that fails to distinguish between lobbyists who worked to enrich narrow corporate interests and those who advocated for broader public goods like human rights or consumer protection.

The result is a paradox: an administration that came into office promising greater efficiency and competence in government has instead found itself hamstrung by its own rules, unable to fully staff the very agencies most needed to address the nation's economic and foreign policy challenges. As the financial crisis deepens and international crises continue to demand attention, the slow pace of nominations and confirmations threatens to undermine the administration's ability to govern effectively, even as it remains committed to the ethical principles that created the bottleneck in the first place.

Whether the White House will revisit or loosen these restrictions remains to be seen. But the situation at Treasury—and the cautionary tale of Tom Malinowski—illustrates a broader challenge facing the Obama administration: the difficulty of turning noble campaign promises into practical, functional policy once the realities of governing set in.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style opinion piece about how Obama's anti-lobbyist ethics rules are backfiring and making it hard to staff his administration, using Geithner and Treasury as the lead example.
counterfactuals.output:
**Obama's Ethics Rules: When Good Intentions Meet Governing Reality**

Barack Obama swept into office promising the most ethically rigorous administration in American history. No more revolving door between K Street and the West Wing. No more lobbyists shaping the very policies they were paid to influence. It was a compelling narrative for a candidate who ran against Washington's culture of insider dealing.

But six weeks into his presidency, that narrative is colliding with an inconvenient truth: you can't run the world's most complex government without hiring people who understand how it actually works—and increasingly, those are exactly the people Obama's rules disqualify.

Exhibit A is Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner's department, which finds itself dangerously understaffed at the precise moment America faces its worst financial crisis in generations. Geithner is supposed to be marshaling a team of senior officials to manage bank bailouts, toxic asset purchases, and a housing crisis spiraling out of control. Instead, he's largely operating a skeleton crew, because many of the qualified candidates for these positions have, at some point, done work that Obama's ethics rules now treat as disqualifying.

The pattern is becoming familiar. A promising nominee is identified. Vetting begins. Then reporters or opposition researchers discover that the candidate once did legal work for a financial firm, or briefly registered as a lobbyist years ago, or sits on the wrong side of Obama's own executive order barring recent lobbyists from working on issues they lobbied on. The nomination stalls or dies. Meanwhile, the empty desk remains empty.

Consider the irony: the financial crisis requires deep expertise in exactly the kind of complex financial instruments and Wall Street mechanics that few people outside the industry possess. The talent pool for these jobs was never enormous. Shrink it further by excluding anyone who's had substantive contact with the financial sector, and you're left fishing in a very small pond during an emergency that demands speed.

This isn't an argument that ethics don't matter. The revolving door problem is real, and voters were right to want change. But there's a difference between smart conflict-of-interest management and a blunt instrument that treats all private-sector experience as inherently corrupting.

The administration now finds itself in the awkward position of granting waivers to its own rules—as it did for Deputy Defense Secretary William Lynn, a former Raytheon lobbyist—undermining the very message of purity the rules were meant to send. Every waiver becomes a story about hypocrisy rather than pragmatism, even when the exception makes obvious sense.

Geithner didn't create this problem, but he's living it daily. Treasury needs a functioning team of assistant secretaries and senior advisers to manage a financial rescue effort of unprecedented scope. Instead, the building echoes with vacancies while markets remain jittery and the administration's economic message gets diluted by an obvious staffing crisis.

The deeper issue is that Obama campaigned on a binary framing—lobbyists bad, everyone else presumptively good—that doesn't survive contact with governing. Expertise in banking, healthcare, energy, and defense often comes hand-in-hand with some connection to the industries being regulated. That's not corruption; it's often just competence.

If the administration wants to solve this problace, it needs to move from rigid categorical bans toward case-by-case judgment: recusal requirements, cooling-off periods, transparency about waivers granted for genuine expertise. The current approach—announce sweeping rules, then quietly carve out exceptions when reality intervenes—satisfies no one. It doesn't deliver on the promise of a lobbyist-free government, and it leaves crucial positions unfilled during a moment when the country can least afford empty chairs at Treasury.

Obama was right that Washington needed a course correction on ethics. But governing well requires more than good intentions and clean rhetoric. It requires actually staffing the government tasked with fixing the biggest economic crisis in generations. Right now, that government is understaffed, and the ethics rules bear real responsibility for why.

# Treasury's Empty Halls: Why Geithner Stands Alone

**WASHINGTON** — More than four months into the Obama administration, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner remains a striking anomaly: the sole Senate-confirmed official running a department tasked with unprecedented economic firefighting. No deputy secretary. No confirmed under secretaries. A skeletal senior staff largely composed of holdovers, advisors on loan, and officials operating in "acting" capacities.

The vacancy is not merely a bureaucratic curiosity — it is a direct consequence of the administration's own ethics policy colliding with the realities of finding qualified financial talent in a moment of crisis.

## The Pledge That Boomeranged

Early in his transition, President Obama imposed some of the strictest lobbying restrictions ever placed on an incoming administration. Registered lobbyists were barred from taking jobs in agencies they had lobbied within the previous two years, and appointees were required to pledge they would not lobby the administration after leaving government.

The rules were designed as a rebuke to the revolving-door culture of Washington and a signal that the new administration would not be captured by the same financial interests it was now regulating. But they have had an unintended side effect: they have narrowed, dramatically, the pool of experienced candidates willing or able to take senior Treasury posts.

Treasury is not just any agency. Its senior roles require deep fluency in derivatives markets, bank regulation, tax policy, and international finance — expertise that, in practice, is concentrated among people who have spent careers on Wall Street, in law firms that lobby on financial policy, or in trade associations representing banks. Many potential nominees have quietly withdrawn from consideration after discovering that old lobbying work, or a spouse's financial ties, created disqualifying conflicts.

## Vetting Under a Microscope

Compounding the lobbying rules is a vetting process that has grown extraordinarily exacting since several early nominees — most notably Tom Daschle — withdrew over unpaid taxes. Treasury nominees now face exhaustive scrutiny of their tax filings, past business dealings, and financial holdings, a process that can take months and that several prospective candidates have simply declined to endure.

The result is a bottleneck. Names are floated, vetted, and in some cases abandoned before a formal nomination is ever made. Administration officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, acknowledge that several candidates for under secretary and assistant secretary posts have dropped out over conflict-of-interest concerns tied directly to the ethics pledge.

## A Department Running on Fumes

In the meantime, Geithner has leaned heavily on a small cadre of counselors and advisors — some brought in as consultants rather than officials requiring confirmation, a workaround that has itself drawn criticism from government watchdogs and Senate Republicans who argue it circumvents the confirmation process entirely.

Critics on the right have seized on the vacancies as evidence of administrative dysfunction at precisely the moment Treasury is managing bank stress tests, the auto industry restructuring, and the disbursement of TARP funds. Critics on the left, meanwhile, worry that the thin bench of confirmed officials leaves Geithner overly reliant on advice from a small circle with ties to the very Wall Street firms at the center of the crisis — the exact dynamic the ethics rules were meant to prevent.

## The Deeper Tension

The Treasury vacancy crisis illustrates a genuine policy tension rather than simple incompetence: the expertise needed to regulate complex financial markets often lives inside the institutions being regulated. Strict anti-revolving-door rules, however well-intentioned, can inadvertently filter out the very people equipped to do the job — or force the administration to grant case-by-case waivers, which carry their own political cost.

The administration has in fact granted a handful of ethics waivers already, drawing accusations of hypocrisy from transparency advocates who argue the rules are being applied selectively.

As the vacancies persist, the episode has become something of a case study in the limits of ethics-by-fiat: rules crafted to restore public trust in government can, if too rigid, end up hollowing out the very agencies the public most needs functioning at full strength.

---

*This analysis reflects reporting circumstances typical of spring 2009; specific personnel details should be verified against contemporaneous sources.*

# The Absurdity of Purity Tests: What the Malinowski Case Reveals About Washington's Broken Ethics Rules

When the Obama administration blocked Tom Malinowski's path to a senior human rights position over his history as a Human Rights Watch lobbyist, it should have prompted a moment of collective embarrassment in Washington. Instead, it barely registered as news—just another data point in the capital's long-running theater of the absurd, where rules designed to combat corruption end up punishing the wrong people entirely.

Let's be clear about who Tom Malinowski is. This is not a former Goldman Sachs executive angling for a banking regulator post, nor a pharmaceutical lobbyist seeking to oversee drug pricing policy. This is a man who spent years advocating for political prisoners, documenting torture, and pushing the U.S. government to take human rights seriously in its foreign policy calculations. His "lobbying" consisted of trying to convince Congress and the executive branch to care more about human dignity abroad—hardly the revolving-door corruption the ban was designed to prevent.

## The Letter of the Law, The Death of Its Spirit

The Obama administration's lobbying ban emerged from legitimate concerns about regulatory capture—the phenomenon where industry insiders cycle through government positions, using public service as a stepping stone to enrich themselves or their former employers. It's a real problem. Financial regulators who previously worked for the banks they're supposed to oversee, energy officials with deep ties to fossil fuel companies, defense officials who shuffle between the Pentagon and contractors—these are legitimate targets for reform.

But somewhere in the drafting of these rules, nuance was sacrificed for the appearance of toughness. The policy made no meaningful distinction between lobbying for Exxon and lobbying for human rights. A blanket ban, applied without judgment about the nature or purpose of the advocacy work, treats all lobbying as morally equivalent—as if pushing for stronger sanctions against dictators is the same species of activity as pushing for tax loopholes.

This is bureaucratic thinking at its most brain-dead: mistaking uniformity for fairness, and rigidity for integrity.

## The Perverse Incentive Structure

Consider what this actually incentivizes. If the price of advocacy work is disqualification from future government service, you're telling talented people that the smart career move is to avoid organizations like Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, or the ACLU. Better to keep your head down at a think tank, or better yet, avoid taking public positions altogether if you ever want a seat at the policymaking table.

This is precisely backwards. We should want people who have spent their careers in the trenches fighting for human rights to eventually have the chance to implement those values from within government. Malinowski's experience lobbying for human rights wasn't a conflict of interest for a human rights position—it was the single most relevant qualification imaginable. It's the equivalent of disqualifying a doctor from a public health post because she once advocated for better healthcare policy.

The message sent to idealistic young people entering public service is clear: advocacy is dangerous. Passion is a liability. If you actually believe in something enough to fight for it professionally, that conviction will be held against you later, while a resume of calculated neutrality will be rewarded.

## Ethics Theater vs. Ethics Substance

What makes this case particularly galling is how it reveals the difference between actual ethics reform and ethics theater. Actual reform would ask serious questions: What was the substance of this person's advocacy? Does it create genuine conflicts with their prospective role? Would their past positions compromise their judgment, or does their expertise make them uniquely qualified?

Ethics theater, by contrast, cares only about optics and box-checking. It doesn't ask whether Malinowski's history posed any real conflict with a human rights post—because the answer is so obviously "no" that asking the question would be absurd. Instead, it applies a mechanical test: Were you a registered lobbyist? Yes or no. The ban becomes a blunt instrument that captures minnows while whales swim past unaffected, because the truly compromised revolving-door operators—the corporate lawyers, the ex-officials-turned-consultants who never had to register as lobbyists—often evade these rules through more sophisticated arrangements anyway.

## The Deeper Irony

There's a bitter irony in an administration that came to office promising to elevate human rights in foreign policy, only to have its own ethics apparatus block one of the country's most credible human rights advocates from serving in exactly that capacity. It's the kind of self-defeating outcome that fuels cynicism about government generally—the sense that Washington's rules exist not to produce good outcomes but to provide political cover, regardless of whether they make any sense in practice.

If the lobbying ban can't distinguish between advocating for torture victims and advocating for tax breaks, then it isn't really an ethics policy at all. It's a crude sorting mechanism that mistakes activity for corruption and inadvertently punishes exactly the kind of committed public servants we should want in government.

Tom Malinowski eventually found his way into government service through other channels, and later into Congress, proving that talent and conviction eventually route around obstacles. But the fact that a good rule producer this bad an outcome should trouble anyone who cares about actually functional government—not government that merely appears clean, but one that intelligently distinguishes between real conflicts of interest and the kind of principled advocacy that should be a *qualification*, not a disqualification, for public service.

The lesson isn't that ethics rules are unnecessary. It's that rules crafted without wisdom, nuance, or good judgment will inevitably produce absurd results—and when they do, the people who suffer aren't the corrupt insiders these rules were meant to stop, but the earnest reformers these rules were never meant to catch.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an in-depth journalistic piece in the voice of a Washington insider correspondent, criticizing the Obama administration's ethics/vetting rules for slowing down appointments, citing examples like William Lynn as a rare exception.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Vetting Vortex: How Obama's Ethics Rules Became Washington's Newest Gridlock

*A Washington Insider's Notebook*

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over the sub-cabinet levels of a new administration when the personnel machine seizes up. It is not the quiet of competence. It is the quiet of empty offices, of acting officials filling roles meant for confirmed appointees, of career staff shrugging when reporters ask who, exactly, is running a given shop. Eighteen months into the Obama presidency, that quiet had become one of this town's worst-kept secrets: the administration that promised to clean up Washington had built an ethics and vetting apparatus so exacting, so risk-averse, that it was strangling its own ability to govern.

The instinct behind it was defensible, even admirable. After the revolving-door excesses of the Bush years, candidate Obama ran on a promise to close the gap between K Street and the West Wing. The resulting executive order — barring lobbyists from serving in agencies they'd lobbied within the previous two years, and barring departing officials from lobbying those same agencies for two years after — was meant to be a bright line. Paired with it came a financial-disclosure questionnaire so exhaustive that veterans of three prior administrations described it, without much exaggeration, as the most invasive document they had ever been asked to fill out: decades of tax returns, every email that might embarrass, every associate who might embarrass, every domestic employee's immigration status, every blog post a spouse might have written in 2003.

The problem is that vetting of this intensity does not merely catch problems. It deters candidates from ever entering the pool. Talented people with complicated, ordinary American financial lives — a rental property, a consulting gig, a nanny paid in cash a decade ago — began quietly declining to be considered rather than subject themselves and their families to months of forensic scrutiny for a job that pays a fraction of what they make in the private sector. Recruiters working the sub-cabinet levels told me, on background, that the questionnaire alone had become a recruiting tool for the private sector: why endure this indignity for an undersecretary's salary when the firm down the street will simply hire you without asking for your college roommate's phone number?

The casualties piled up fast enough to become their own subplot of the administration's first year. Tom Daschle, the presumptive Health and Human Services secretary, withdrew after back taxes on a car service surfaced — a sum so comparatively modest that longtime Hill hands marveled it was enough to sink a nomination. Nancy Killefer, tapped to be the government's first chief performance officer, withdrew over a tax lien connected to household help before she'd even been formally nominated. Timothy Geithner survived his own tax troubles only because Treasury could not plausibly be left without a secretary in the middle of a financial collapse — proof, if any were needed, that the rules were rules until the stakes were high enough to bend them.

Which brings us to William J. Lynn.

Lynn's nomination as deputy secretary of defense was, on paper, precisely the kind of appointment the ethics pledge was designed to prevent. He had spent years as Raytheon's chief Washington lobbyist, shuttling between the Pentagon's budget process and the interests of one of its largest contractors — the very "revolving door" the administration had vowed to weld shut. And yet Lynn got his waiver. The White House granted him an exception on the grounds that his expertise was too valuable to lose, that the Pentagon's incoming leadership needed someone who understood the building's budget architecture from the inside.

Perhaps that was even true. Lynn went on to serve competently, by most accounts, overseeing cyber policy and acquisition reform during a difficult stretch for the department. But the waiver did something the administration's press shop never quite reckoned with: it exposed the entire ethics architecture as negotiable precisely at the moment it mattered most. If the rule could be waived for a defense lobbyist deemed indispensable, the message to every other capable, imperfect candidate sitting on the sidelines was unambiguous. The rules were not a floor. They were a toll booth, and some people were simply waved through.

That double message — rigid to the point of dysfunction for the many, flexible for the few deemed essential — is arguably worse than either extreme rules or none at all. It leaves qualified people who might have accepted appointments concluding, not unreasonably, that the process is arbitrary rather than principled. And it leaves agencies second-guessing whether the vacancy in front of them is worth the year-long slog of clearances, background checks, financial disclosures, and Senate holds that now stands between a president's decision to appoint someone and that person's first day on the job.

The numbers tell their own story. More than a year into the term, hundreds of sub-cabinet and agency posts requiring Senate confirmation remained unfilled — not because of Republican obstruction alone, though there was plenty of that, but because nominations were taking months to even clear the White House's own internal review before a name ever reached the Senate. Agencies charged with implementing the administration's signature initiatives, from financial reform to health care, were doing so with skeleton crews of acting officials lacking the authority or standing to make consequential decisions.

None of this is to argue that ethics standards for public service are a bad idea, or that the instinct to keep lobbyists out of the agencies they once worked to influence is misguided. It is to observe, as this town has now watched play out in real time, that a system engineered entirely around risk avoidance will inevitably avoid the risk of hiring anyone at all — until, that is, the administration needs someone badly enough to look past the very standard it set for everyone else. William Lynn did not have to answer for years he spent inside Raytheon's Washington operation the way a mid-level nominee for an obscure regulatory post had to answer for a decade-old parking ticket. That asymmetry, more than any single withdrawn nomination, is the real indictment of how this White House chose to vet the people meant to run its government.

The lesson of the first eighteen months was not that ethics rules are unnecessary. It was that rules applied with maximum rigidity to the powerless and maximum flexibility to the powerful are not ethics rules at all. They are, in the oldest Washington tradition, simply another set of rules for insiders to navigate — only this time, the insiders wrote them themselves.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN.com opinion column arguing that overly broad restrictions on hiring former lobbyists are preventing qualified experts from joining the government, ultimately hurting Obama's ability to respond to the economic crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
# When Good Intentions Undermine Good Government

*The following is an opinion piece in the style of commentary that appeared during debates over Obama-era ethics rules*

When President Obama took office amid the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, he made a promise that resonated with a public disgusted by Washington's revolving door: no more business as usual. Executive Order 13490 banned former lobbyists from working on issues they'd lobbied on for two years, and barred them from federal agencies they'd targeted altogether.

The intent was noble. The execution has been costly.

Consider the math. The people who understand financial derivatives, healthcare reimbursement structures, or telecommunications spectrum policy in granular detail are, disproportionately, the people who've spent careers working on these issues—often as advocates for industry, nonprofits, or unions. That's not corruption. That's expertise. By defining "lobbyist" so broadly and the restriction so absolutely, the administration has effectively told itself: we will not hire the people who know the most about the problems we're trying to solve.

This isn't hypothetical. Treasury and other agencies scrambling to design responses to the financial meltdown needed people who understood credit default swaps, mortgage-backed securities, and bank balance sheets—not in the abstract, but from having worked the actual deals. Some of the most qualified candidates for these roles have direct industry experience that technically classifies them as "lobbyists" under the rule, even if their work bore little resemblance to the stereotype of a fixer buying influence on K Street.

The policy also creates perverse incentives. It doesn't eliminate industry influence—it just launders it. Instead of hiring a transparent, registered lobbyist who has to disclose contacts and clients, agencies hire someone who did the *same substantive work* but never formally registered, or they rely more heavily on outside consultants and contractors who face no such restrictions at all. The government loses accountability while gaining nothing in terms of actual independence from industry perspective.

There's also a matter of intellectual honesty. Many of the "lobbyists" caught in this net were pushing for things like stronger financial regulations, patient protections, or environmental standards—hardly the caricature of corporate influence-peddling that justified the rule in the first place. A blanket ban doesn't distinguish between someone who lobbied for tobacco companies to gut regulations and someone who lobbied for consumer groups to strengthen them.

None of this means the revolving door isn't a real problem, or that Obama was wrong to want change. But blunt instruments create blunt consequences. A more calibrated approach—case-by-case waivers, recusal from specific matters rather than blanket agency bans, disclosure requirements instead of prohibition—could have preserved the goal of reducing improper influence while not starving the administration of talent precisely when it needed expertise most urgently.

The economic crisis demanded the best minds available, regardless of their résumé's proximity to K Street. Good governance requires judgment, not just rules—and right now, the rules are getting in the way.

---

*Note: I've written this as a persuasive opinion piece reflecting a genuine policy debate that existed at the time, but I want to flag that this represents one side of a contested issue. Many ethics experts and government reformers argued the opposite—that the restrictions were reasonable and necessary, and that talented experts without industry ties were available. I can help you explore counterarguments or historical context if useful.*
